newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan ethnic group sees power share in Sindh.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan ethnic group sees power share in Sindh.

text.p: Pakistani elections have given the ethnic Mohajir National Movement (MQM) a new chance to share power in Sindh province after years of conflict with security forces, party sources and analysts said on Thursday.
With no single party emerging from Monday's polls with a decisive majority, the MQM has been courted by other parties eyeing the possibility of forming a coalition government in the restive province.
"All the rest of the parties and groups have contacted us for the formation of government in Sindh," MQM spokesman Kunwar Khalid Younus told Reuters. "We are now weighing our options."
He said the MQM, which speaks for Urdu-speaking people who migrated from the rest of India at its Partition in 1947, would be a major partner in the future Sindh government.

The volatile southern province has been a traditional home power base for ousted prime minister Benazir Bhutto, whose Pakistan People's Party (PPP) suffered a crushing defeat in Monday's vote for the 217-seat National Assembly (lower house) and four provincial assemblies.

The PPP, routed by the Pakistan Muslim League (PML) of former prime minister Nawaz Sharif nationally and in two other provinces that it previously ruled, still remains the largest party in the 109-seat Sindh assembly with 36 seats.
However, it remains far short of a simple majority and has little chance of finding a major coalition partner.
In the 1993 elections, the PPP won 56 seats, well ahead of the MQM with 27 seats and the PML which held eight seats.
The MQM made a slight improvement in its position on Monday, winning 28 seats, and the PML's share jumped to 14 seats.
A PML spokesman said it would try to form a coalition government in Sindh, where 14 seats have gone to independents and others to smaller groups.
"The MQM is our natural ally in Sindh, we have contacted its leadership for the formation of the provincial government," a PML National Assembly deputy, Haleem Siddiqui, said.
Both the MQM and PML oppose Bhutto's PPP.
Newspaper reports said the PPP had also contacted the MQM, but an alliance between them appeared unlikey.
The PPP will not be allowed to form a coalition government in Sindh, said Imran Aslam, the editor of The News daily.
"It is sad that the PPP has been transformed into a regional party and its national stature has been destroyed, which is also a negative for the Sindh province."

The MQM has suffered a major security crackdown under the governments of both Sharif and Bhutto since 1992, with authorities blaming it for most of the ethnic violence in Karachi, Pakistan's commercial hub.
But the group maintained contact with Sharif in recent months after the PML joined it in accusing Bhutto's government of excesses against MQM activists and extra-judicial killings.

Bhutto, whose three-year-old government was sacked by President Farooq Leghari in November on disputed charges of misrule, has called Monday's elections rigged but says she will not agitate against the poll for the sake of stability.
